title: Loans
in30Seconds: A loan is money borrowed that is repaid over time, usually with interest. The borrower gets the funds up front and promises to pay back the principal — the amount borrowed — plus interest, in regular payments over a set period called the term. Loans come in two useful pairs: secured or unsecured, and installment or revolving. The true cost of any loan is interest plus any fees, and comparing loans means comparing rate, term, and fees. In plain terms, a loan trades future income for present needs.
whyItMatters: Almost every household borrows at some point, and loans are how most people handle purchases too large for one paycheck. Knowing the parts — principal, interest, term, payment — is the difference between reading a loan offer and guessing at it. It matters academically because loan mechanics reappear in economics, accounting, and finance courses. And it matters forward-looking: the same vocabulary and comparisons show up in credit cards, auto loans, student loans, and mortgages, so understanding loans now makes every later credit decision clearer.
learningObjectives: Define a loan as money borrowed that is repaid over time, usually with interest, and name its four parts: principal, interest, term, and payment.
Distinguish a secured loan, backed by collateral, from an unsecured loan, backed only by the borrower's promise and creditworthiness.
Distinguish an installment loan, repaid in fixed payments over a set term, from revolving credit, which can be borrowed again as it is repaid.
Explain that the total cost of a loan is interest plus any fees.
Identify what to compare across loans — rate, term, and fees — stated factually, without advice.
Apply the honest framing that a loan trades future income for present needs.

collegeVersion.heading: Borrowed money with a repayment plan
collegeVersion.body: A loan is money borrowed that is repaid over time, usually with interest. That working definition matches how official sources describe the arrangement: the SEC's Investor.gov glossary defines debt as an amount owed for borrowed funds, normally repaid with interest on a schedule set out in the repayment terms; MyMoney.gov, the U.S. Treasury's financial-education site, describes borrowing as a way to purchase something now and pay for it over time; and the Corporate Finance Institute defines a loan as a sum of money borrowed that is paid back with interest within a given period. Every loan has four parts. The principal is the amount borrowed, on which interest is calculated — borrow $2,400 and the principal is $2,400. The interest is the price paid for borrowing, quoted as a percentage per period — 8 percent per year in this example. The term is the length of the repayment period — here, 36 months. The payment is the periodic amount the borrower pays, typically covering the interest charged plus a slice of the principal — $75.21 a month on this loan. Repay all four parts and the loan is done.

collegeVersion.heading: Secured versus unsecured: collateral versus promise
collegeVersion.body: Loans divide first by what backs them. A secured loan is backed by collateral: an asset the borrower pledges, such as a car or a home, that the lender can take if the loan is not repaid. An unsecured loan has no collateral; the lender relies on the borrower's promise to pay, along with credit history and income. Example: Priya borrows $4,000 for a kitchen repair and pledges her car as collateral — if she stops paying, the lender can repossess the car. Her cousin borrows the same $4,000 with no collateral, and the lender has only the cousin's promise and credit record to rely on. Because collateral reduces the lender's risk, secured loans commonly carry lower interest rates than unsecured ones, and unsecured borrowing, such as a personal line of credit, depends on the borrower's creditworthiness. Mortgages and auto loans are everyday secured loans; each is covered in its own sibling lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: Installment versus revolving: fixed payments versus flexible credit
collegeVersion.body: The second classification is about how repayment works. An installment loan — also called a closed-end loan — gives the borrower all of the money at the beginning and is repaid in set, fixed amounts over a specific period; the payment is generally the same every month until the loan ends. A revolving account, by contrast, sets a credit limit, sends a monthly bill, asks for at least a minimum payment, and charges interest on whatever balance is outstanding; as the balance is paid down, the credit becomes available again, up to the limit. Credit cards are the most common example of revolving credit — the credit-cards lesson in this series is a sibling topic, so this lesson only names the distinction. Installment loans can run from a few hundred dollars repaid over months to large sums repaid over several years, and the fixed payment holds for the life of the loan.

collegeVersion.heading: What a loan really costs: interest plus fees
collegeVersion.body: The true cost of a loan is interest plus any fees. CFPB guidance on installment loans lists fees that can be added on top of interest: an origination fee for setting up the loan, a documentation fee for processing the paperwork, credit insurance (generally optional), and late fees. Together they raise the total. MyMoney.gov explains the summary figure: the annual percentage rate, or APR, is the total cost — interest charges and fees — described as a yearly rate. Example: Lena borrows $1,200 with a 12-month term. Her payment is $106 a month, which repays the $1,200 plus $72 in interest, and the lender adds a $40 origination fee up front — so the loan costs her $112 beyond the $1,200 she borrowed. The interest part of that cost belongs to the sibling lesson on interest; the point here is the total.

collegeVersion.heading: Comparing loans, and the honest trade underneath
collegeVersion.body: When loans are compared, three features matter, stated factually: the rate, the term, and the fees. CFPB guidance on shopping for credit says to look at the annual percentage rate, whether and how much the rate can change, and any fees — for accessing the credit, annual fees, late-payment fees, and fees for other events — and to compare costs with other credit options. Both CFPB and MyMoney.gov note that it pays to shop around and compare offers from multiple lenders. The longer the term, the more interest a loan accumulates, because interest is charged for more time. Underneath all of it is an honest trade: borrowing is a way to purchase something now and pay for it over time. A loan trades future income for present needs — the payments come out of paychecks not yet earned. Product-by-product detail (auto loans, student loans, mortgages) and strategies for managing debt belong to their own sibling lessons.

vocabulary.definition: Money borrowed that is repaid over time, usually with interest.
The amount of money borrowed, on which interest is calculated.
The price paid for borrowing money, quoted as a percentage per period.
The length of time a borrower has to repay a loan.
A periodic amount paid on a loan, typically covering interest plus part of the principal.
An asset a borrower pledges to back a loan, which the lender may take if the loan is not repaid.
A loan backed by collateral that the lender can take if the loan is not repaid.
A loan with no collateral, resting on the borrower's promise and creditworthiness.
A closed-end loan repaid in fixed payments over a set term.
An account with a credit limit that can be borrowed again as the balance is repaid.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A loan is borrowed money with a repayment plan. Someone lends you a sum now — the principal — and you pay it back over time in regular payments, each one covering some interest plus part of the principal. Interest is the lender's charge for letting you use the money, and the term is how long the plan runs. Loans come in two useful pairs: a secured loan is backed by something you own, while an unsecured loan is not; an installment loan is paid in fixed amounts until the balance hits zero, while revolving credit lets you borrow again as you pay down. The real cost is interest plus any fees, which is why comparing loans means comparing rate, term, and fees. At bottom, a loan lets you spend future income today.
eli10.analogy: Borrowing is like borrowing a ladder from a neighbor: you get the ladder now to finish the job, use it, and give it back. A loan works the same way — you get the money now, use it, and give the money back — except this ladder comes with a rental fee: interest, charged for every month you keep it. And a lender is pickier than a neighbor: for a secured loan, the lender keeps a claim on something you own until the money is fully returned.
eli10.analogyLimits: A neighbor lends a ladder for free, charges nothing for the time it sits in your yard, and would never take your car if you forget to return it. A lender charges interest for the whole time the money is out, can add fees on top, and for a secured loan can take the collateral if you stop paying. And a borrowed ladder is returned whole, while a loan is repaid with more money than you received — the difference is the price of using it.

workedExample: Maya's water heater fails, and she borrows $1,500 from her credit union to replace it. The loan carries a 9% annual interest rate and a 24-month term, repaid in fixed monthly payments. Her payment is $68.53: each month's payment covers the interest charged on the remaining principal plus a slice of the principal itself. Over 24 months she pays $1,644.65 in total — the $1,500 principal plus about $145 in interest. On top of that, the lender charges a $50 origination fee when the loan is set up, so the loan costs her about $195 more than the $1,500 she received. Same payment every month, term fixed at 24 months, and the balance moves in one direction only: down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the monthly payment as the cost of the loan.
commonMistakes.correction: The payment is one slice of the cost. The total is the payment multiplied by the number of payments — interest and fees on top of principal. Lena's $106 monthly payment on a 12-month loan added up to $112 of interest and fees beyond the $1,200 borrowed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a smaller monthly payment means a cheaper loan.
commonMistakes.correction: A longer term shrinks the monthly payment but stretches the interest over more time, so the total cost can rise. Comparing loans means comparing the whole package — rate, term, and fees — not just the payment.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating revolving credit like an installment loan.
commonMistakes.correction: An installment loan has fixed payments and a balance that only goes down. With revolving credit, paying down the balance frees up the limit, and the balance can rise again.

commonMistakes.mistake: Comparing only interest rates and ignoring fees.
commonMistakes.correction: Origination, documentation, and late fees all add to the total cost. The APR bundles interest charges and fees into one yearly figure, which is why it is the standard number to compare.

compareContrast.distinction: A secured loan is backed by collateral the lender can take if the loan is not repaid; an unsecured loan is backed only by the borrower's promise and creditworthiness.
An installment loan pays a fixed balance down to zero with fixed payments; revolving credit has a limit, and repaid amounts become available to borrow again.
The principal is the amount borrowed; the total cost is everything the borrower actually pays back — principal plus interest plus any fees.

keyTakeaway: A loan is borrowed money with a repayment plan: principal repaid with interest over a set term in regular payments, at a true cost of interest plus any fees. Every loan trades future income for present needs, so comparing rate, term, and fees matters more than any single number.

questionBank.prompt: In a loan, what is the principal?
options: The interest rate charged on the loan
The amount of money borrowed, on which interest is calculated
The total fees the lender charges
The number of months the borrower has to repay
questionBank.explanation: The principal is the amount borrowed, and interest is calculated on it. The interest rate is a percentage charged on the principal, fees are separate charges, and the repayment length is the term.

questionBank.prompt: How does a secured loan differ from an unsecured loan?
options: A secured loan is backed by collateral the lender can take if the loan is not repaid; an unsecured loan is not backed by collateral
A secured loan charges no interest; an unsecured loan charges interest
A secured loan is repaid in a single payment; an unsecured loan is repaid monthly
A secured loan may only be used for a vehicle; an unsecured loan may be used for anything
questionBank.explanation: The dividing line is collateral: a secured loan is backed by an asset the borrower pledges, while an unsecured loan rests on the borrower's promise and creditworthiness. Both types charge interest, and either can be repaid on any schedule.

questionBank.prompt: Lena borrows $1,200 with a 12-month term. Her monthly payment is $106, and the lender charges a $40 origination fee up front. How much does the loan cost her in interest and fees combined?
questionBank.explanation: Twelve payments of $106 total $1,272, which is $72 of interest on top of the $1,200 principal. Adding the $40 origination fee gives $112 — the total cost beyond the amount borrowed.
questionBank.skill: computing the total cost of a loan as interest plus fees

questionBank.prompt: Two lenders offer $5,000 loans at the same interest rate. Lender A's term is 24 months; Lender B's term is 60 months. Which statement about the two loans is true?
options: Lender A's loan will have higher monthly payments but less total interest
Lender B's loan will have lower monthly payments and less total interest
The two loans will cost exactly the same amount
Lender B's loan charges no interest for the first year
questionBank.explanation: A shorter term spreads the repayment over fewer months, so each payment is larger, but interest is charged for less time, so the total interest is smaller. Lender B's longer term means more total interest, and nothing in the prompt waives interest for any period.
questionBank.skill: analyzing how the term affects monthly payments and total interest

questionBank.prompt: Which situation describes revolving credit rather than an installment loan?
options: A borrower repays the same fixed amount every month until the balance reaches zero
A borrower has a credit limit, repays part of the balance, and can borrow again up to the limit
A borrower pledges a car as collateral for the loan
A borrower receives the full loan amount in a single payment at the start
questionBank.explanation: Revolving credit is open-end: repaid amounts free up the credit limit and can be borrowed again. Fixed payments to zero describe an installment loan, pledging collateral describes a secured loan, and receiving the full amount up front describes a closed-end loan.
questionBank.skill: recognizing revolving credit as distinct from an installment loan

provenance.rightsStatus: reference-only sources (U.S. government pages and one CFI explainer); all prose, examples, and figures are original
provenance.transformation: Lesson synthesized from live CFPB Ask CFPB pages (en-2114, en-2120, en-901, en-905), MyMoney.gov's Borrow page, the SEC Investor.gov glossary (principal, interest, liability/debt), and the CFI loan explainer, all read on 2026-08-21. The working definition, the four parts, both classification pairs, the total-cost idea (interest plus fees, APR), and the comparing list (rate, term, fees) are grounded in those sources; every example, scenario, and dollar figure is original and arithmetic was independently computed.
